title: The three watches
hookLine: first watch, his past lives; second, beings passing by their deeds; third, the ending of the taints (MN 36)
last: BHŪMISPARŚA — THE EARTH IS YOUR WITNESS.

cards: A night awake, with a newborn, in a hospital, at a vigil, on a night shift, isn't one thing. There's the early part, when you're still yourself. The deep middle, when the world goes strange and quiet.
And the last hours, gray and thin, when something shifts before the light comes. The sutta that tells this night divides it into three watches, like guard shifts. Mara is gone.
The wanderer is alone with the dark, and his mind, he says, is calm, clear and steady. Now the real work of the night begins.

teach.h: FIRST WATCH — HIS OWN PAST LIVES.
teach.b: The Buddha describes this night himself, in the same sutta where he told of the austerities.

In the first watch, his settled mind turned to memory, and he recalled his past lives: one birth, two, a hundred, a hundred thousand, across the ages. Here I had this name, this family, this food, these joys and pains.
There I died, and was born again. Like a traveler remembering every village on a long road. In the second watch, he turned outward.

teach.h: SECOND — ALL BEINGS AND THEIR DEEDS.
teach.b: He saw beings everywhere dying and being reborn, and he saw why: they fare according to their actions, kind ones leading one way, cruel ones another.
Kamma, the law of action and result, laid open like a landscape seen from a hilltop. In the third watch, the last before dawn, he turned to the root of it all.
He saw suffering, its cause, its ending, and the way to its ending, directly.

teach.h: THIRD — THE TAINTS COME TO AN END.
teach.b: And he saw the taints, the deep stains of sensual desire, becoming and ignorance, come to an end. Ignorance was gone, he says; knowledge arose.
Darkness was gone; light arose. Notice the order: his own story, then everyone's story, then the thing underneath every story. Buddhists read this in different ways.
Traditional teaching takes the past lives as the Buddha's direct memory; some modern readers focus more on the pattern the night reveals.
Either way, the text keeps the shape: the night had watches, and each one went deeper.

how: Buddhists teach the three knowledges of the awakening night (past lives, the passing of beings according to kamma, and the ending of the taints), and some communities keep all-night vigils of meditation on the anniversary of the awakening.

games.q: it's the last watch before dawn. you've seen your own past lives and all beings passing by their deeds. where does your mind turn now?
o: to the root: suffering, its cause, its ending.
to sleep: it's been a long night.
games.why: in the third watch he sees the four truths directly and the taints end. darkness is gone; light arises.

practice: Take three slow breaths, one for each watch: on the first, look inward at your own body and mood; on the second, look outward at the people around you, each with their own story, their own actions and results; on the third, look underneath, at the simple fact of breathing beneath every story.
Then keep sitting, watching the breath arrive and leave.

wordCard.voice: Asava. The deep taints, of desire, becoming and ignorance, that ended in the last of the three watches under the tree.

orig.note: Pali: a taint, an outflow; the deep stains (of sensual desire, becoming and ignorance) that end in the third watch.

carryVoice: Your line: night has watches. A hard stretch has parts too. Day fifty-four, done.
